children: By Blake Brittain

A group of musicians including renowned singer-songwriter Jason Isbell has filed a class-action lawsuit against AI music generator Suno in Massachusetts federal court for allegedly violating their publicity rights.

Isbell, singer David Lowery of the rock bands Cracker and Camper Van Beethoven, blues musician Guy Forsyth and saxophonist Eduardo Calle said in their lawsuit filed on Monday that Suno used their identities without permission to enable users to create songs in their style.
The lawsuit is the latest in a wave of cases brought against tech companies by authors, publishers, news outlets and others over the use of their work to train
systems.

Unlike many music-related AI training cases, which were brought by labels and focus on the alleged misuse of lyrics, compositions and sound recordings under copyright law, the artists' proposed class action against Suno focuses on their name, image and likeness rights.

"Many musicians sell their rights to specific recordings. However, the identity right belongs to the performer regardless of who owns any copyright in an underlying recording," the lawsuit said. "This lawsuit seeks to recover the value of those misappropriated identities and to stop their ongoing commercial exploitation."
Suno said in a statement that it believes the claims lack merit and will defend against the lawsuit.

"Suno exists to help people create new, original music, not to trade on anyone's name," the company said. "We stand by the many protections we have put into place across the platform, including blocking prompts for specific artists' names or copyrighted songs."
An attorney for the musicians declined to comment on the filing.
The lawsuit alleges that Suno falsely claims its users cannot enter musicians' names as prompts.
"In reality, Suno not only accepts names but also responds to the name with an output based on that musician’s identity," the complaint said.

The lawsuit said Suno responded to a prompt with Jason Isbell's name with an Americana song called "Paper Bell" that imitates his "characteristic clear male vocals and country twang." The complaint also named several other artists Suno allegedly imitated on command, including the other plaintiffs, Carly Simon, Buddy Guy and rappers Common and Chief Keef.
The musicians requested an unspecified amount of monetary damages and a court order blocking Suno from using their likenesses.
The case is Isbell v. Suno Inc, U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, No. 1:26-cv-14005.
For the musicians: George Zelcs, Marc Wallenstein and Audrey Austin of Korein Tillery
For Suno: not yet available
